title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
description: Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget n
body: Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month. The yield on a 30-year gilt — a loan to the British government — rose to 5.89%, the highest since 1998.The effective cost of borrowing for governments across the globe has continued to rise this morning with new multi-decade highs in market interest rates.The moves reflect concerns about inflation arising from the ongoing Iran war, competition from major tech firms for long-term borrowing, and concerns about state borrowing levels.Follow live: Burnham addresses MPs for first time as PMAll of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor John Healey. Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock" as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis will be "fiscal responsibility".He said the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living. Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs."Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis. Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days.The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor Rachel Reeves that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing. The more that is forecast to be spent on interest costs, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.The moves in interest rates could already wipe out half of the room for manoeuvre to meet these rules forecast at the last set of official numbers last March.On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.The tax and spend balance in act was already tricky due to extra spending pressures on defence and the cost of living. These moves make these balancing acts trickier still.Global markets reacted in particular after suggestions in the US that its central bank could raise rates. The UK market was closed for the bank holiday yesterday. Japan is also facing pressure to raise rates.The Chancellor is in the USA attending a meeting of global finance ministers and central bankers. He told the G20 that the UK had the fastest growth in the G7 in 2026 so far, that productivity was improving and that the UK was cutting its borrowing at the fastest rate of the major economies.JP Morgan's chief market strategist for Europe, Karen Ward, said governments around the world want to increase spending and are turning to borrowing to fund it.And she told the BBC's World at One they are increasingly having to compete with major technology companies raising money to invest in the AI revolution, pushing up the amount of interest being charged."Markets are getting a lot more choice about who they are going to lend to and at what interest rates," she added.Burnham has rolled out a series of interventions to support consumers and businesses since entering Downing Street, and is expected to prioritise further measures to ease the cost of living in the Budget on 28 October. Ward urged Burnham and Healey to set out how they will fund any fresh spending on defence and the cost of living, and how those lending the government money will be paid back.Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment company XTB, told the BBC News Channel: "Of course, this is red lights flashing.""We are used to pockets of volatility, it has been volatile few months," she says.But record levels of government debt and a record tax take mean "these are not comfortable times for the new government and the new chancellor," she says.Every time bond yields rise, the UK has to pay more on the debt interest, she says.

schema.headline: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget

title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
description: Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.The move will trigger a
body: Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament."He has given this country an lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added. "His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world."I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. "It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wished Sir Keir the best for the future adding: "I can understand why he would not want to spend time with the Labour MPs who treated him so badly after he won them their seats."Tory Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Sir Keir of making "another U-turn having pledged to stay on", prompting a "costly by-election for taxpayers".A date will not be set for the by-election until Sir Keir formally resigns his Commons seat. Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, with Sir Keir securing a more than 11,000-vote majority at the last general election in 2024.Labour's main challenger in the seat is likely to be the Greens, who came second by vote totals at this year's local elections in wards that make up the constituency - with 29.8% of the vote to Labour's 39.5%.Reform UK came a distant third by these vote totals, and the Greens' share was higher if they are given the votes in two wards where they stood aside.Candidates for the by-election will not be confirmed until a later stage, but the Greens hinted that leader Zack Polanski was considering a run at the seat.A spokesperson for the party said Polanksi, currently a member of the London Assembly, had "always made it clear he would like to be a London MP".

schema.headline: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP

title: Times Square stabbing: Woman killed and suspect shot dead by police
description: A 32-year-old woman has been killed and another victim is in hospital following a double stabbing in Times Square, New York late on Monday afternoon.T
body: A 32-year-old woman has been killed and another victim is in hospital following a double stabbing in Times Square, New York late on Monday afternoon.The suspect, a woman wielding two knives, was shot by police. All three people were taken to hospital, where the female victim and the suspect were later pronounced dead, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told a news conference. The deceased victim was later identified as Erin Piacenti, a Bank of America employee. The male victim remains in a stable condition.New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch described the attack as "unprovoked" and said the stabbings took place 20 seconds apart.Citing preliminary information, Tisch said the NYPD call centre received several 911 calls at approximately 16:24 local time (21:00 BST) reporting a woman armed with two knives was stabbing people along Seventh Avenue in Times Square.Police believe the incident began near West 41st Street and Seventh Ave, in Midtown Manhattan.The suspect approached a man who had just exited the subway and was standing with his wife waiting to cross the street, Tisch told a news conference."A witness at the scene told investigators that he observed the subject remove two knives from a red Target bag before approaching the first victim. "The subject waved the knives before stabbing a 68-year-old man in the right side of his abdomen, in what appears to be a random and unprovoked attack." The 68-year-old was taken to Bellevue Hospital and is now stable.The suspect continued up Seventh Avenue towards 42nd Street, which is where she stabbed the second victim, Piacenti, who did not survive after being taken to hospital.Bank of America said in a statement to the BBC: "We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones."The suspect continued on Seventh Avenue, which is when police tried to get her to drop her weapons, speaking to her for four minutes, the NYPD commissioner said."During the encounter she told the officers 'I'm not dropping anything, I'd rather kill both of you'. She repeated 'I will kill you'," Tisch said. The suspect waved knives towards the officers, who then used Tasers, which were "ineffective" and did not stop her from heading towards them.NYPD officers then shot the woman, who was later also pronounced dead at Bellevue Hospital.The suspect was later identified as 49-year-old Pamela Cisneros of Queens, New York City. She had never previously been arrested but had a "documented mental health history with the NYPD, with one incident in 2018 and one in 2019", Tisch added.A tourist from Boston, Melinda Puzon, told the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News that she heard the shots and saw "so many people on the street"."It's very shocking."Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that the incident happened on Monday after a previous version said it was on Wednesday

schema.headline: Times Square stabbing: Woman killed and suspect shot dead by police

title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
description: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spe
body: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported, external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina. The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine soldiers.Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

schema.headline: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review

title: Man in court after Grangetown fire in which woman and niece died
description: A 23-year-old man has appeared in court charged with murdering a woman and her seven-year-old niece who died in a house fire.Natalie McDonald, 34, die
body: A 23-year-old man has appeared in court charged with murdering a woman and her seven-year-old niece who died in a house fire.Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August, along with Valentina Foster.Jaden Wright appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with two counts of murder as well as multiple grievous bodily harm offences.Wright, of no fixed address, was remanded in custody during the hearing that lasted less than two minutes, and is next due to appear at Teesside Crown Court on Thursday.He is also accused of two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent.These charges relate to the six people in the house at the time of the blaze.No pleas were entered during the hearing on Tuesday morning.

schema.headline: Man in court after Grangetown fire in which woman and niece died

title: Newcastle transfer: Matias Fernandez-Pardo joins from Lille for initial £51.4m
description: Newcastle United have signed forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille for an initial £51.4m.Fernandez-Pardo flew into Tyneside on Monday night to hav
body: Newcastle United have signed forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille for an initial £51.4m.Fernandez-Pardo flew into Tyneside on Monday night to have a medical and sign a long-term contract.The 21-year-old said he was "very proud to be at such a big club" following talks with head coach Matthias Jaissle."He really showed how much he wanted me to be here," the Belgium international said. "In terms of my own career progression, it made complete sense to come so I didn't hesitate at all.  "I know the club, I know about the stadium, I know it's a fantastic atmosphere. I've followed the team."I'm still young, I'm still hungry, and that's why I'm here, and I want to make that progress with Newcastle. I can't wait to start the wonderful adventure here."Fernandez-Pardo was left out of Lille's squad for the 2-2 draw against Paris St-Germain last week and ordered to train away from the first-team squad until his future was resolved.The forward has been a long-standing target of Newcastle's - dating back to former head coach Eddie Howe's time in charge - and fits the age range the club have been targeting.Of those players aged 21 and under across Europe's big five leagues last season, Fernandez-Pardo ranked second for big chances (21), fifth for touches in the opposition box (184) and shots on target (30), and seventh for goals and assists combined (13).His ability to play in a number of positions across the frontline also made him an attractive target as Jaissle looked to strengthen his squad."Matias is a highly technical player with explosiveness in his game," Jaissle said. "He can score and assist, he has courage, and he has the ability to take players on. "We're sure our supporters will enjoy watching him play. He has already shown in Lille that he can perform on the big stage, and we will work closely with him to keep developing his game further. "We are excited to see him in a Newcastle United shirt."

schema.headline: Newcastle transfer: Matias Fernandez-Pardo joins from Lille for initial £51.4m

title: Breaker Raygun on processing what happened at Paris 2024 Olympics
description: Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.Thru
body: Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut."I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team."I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself."Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack"."It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been."It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said."You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health."I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency."It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport."It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."After it was announced that breaking would be included at Paris 2024, Gunn qualified to represent her country via the Oceania Breaking Championships in Sydney in 2023."I've never participated in anything of such high stakes before. It was all international judges, but I was relieved and excited when I qualified. And then the next whirlwind happened," she said.Quickly, she realised that she would have to start living like an athlete. Gunn gained a scholarship at the New South Wales Institute of Sport in February 2024, which allowed her to begin a strength and conditioning programme."That was great, but also overwhelming because I was training with people who had been doing that stuff since they were kids," she said.In the midst of her training, the documentary reveals that Gunn's mother suffered three brain aneurisms. Gunn herself began a course of anti-depressants to help with feelings of anxiety.The film portrays how it began to dawn on her what she had taken on when she entered competitions in the run up to the Games."That's when it first starting occurring to me that I was going to be going up against world champs and people who had been winning competitions on big stages for years and years, but I was still going to go out there and do my best," she says in the documentary.In that context, Gunn decided to play to her own strengths with a creative gamble, developing a routine that paid cheeky homage to her Australian roots."I was aware that I was never going to beat my competitors on athleticism," she explained."For me, my strength is creativity. With that being one of the [judging] criteria, our thinking was, 'why don't we put all our eggs in that basket and really try and wow them? Maybe we can make a moment.' "We never, ever expected the impact it might have."The documentary reveals that head of the Australian Breaking Association, Lowe Napalan, only assisted Gunn's training "a handful" of times in the build-up to the Games, owing to the amount of administrative work taking up his time.That meant that he only saw Gunn's controversial routine for the first time just before she performed at the Olympics."I was there side-stage," Napalan says in the film."I had to not have a face of shock."It was reported in November 2024 that the furore around her Olympic performance had led Gunn to quit breaking.She corrects that notion."I don't know where that came from," Gunn said."I wouldn't let what happened take dancing away from me. I love breaking, I'll always break, I'll always be a part of the community."Her hope is that the release of the upcoming film can help shift the conversation."It feels nice to lay it all out there and now be able to look to the future. I'm actually excited about what's to come, which is the first time for a while," she said.Details of organisations offering help and support with mental health are available at bbc.co.uk/actionline

schema.headline: Breaker Raygun on processing what happened at Paris 2024 Olympics

title: Aston Villa complete Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis signings
description: Aston Villa have completed the signings of Senegal winger Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris St-Germain and English centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis from South
body: Aston Villa have completed the signings of Senegal winger Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris St-Germain and English centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis from Southampton.Mbaye, 18, arrives from Paris St-Germain for a fee of 55m euros (£47m), while Villa could pay up to £29m for Harwood-Bellis.Villa have paid an initial fee of £25m - with £4m in potential add-ons - for the 24-year-old defender after seeing two previous bids rejected.Mbaye scored three goals and provided two assists in 31 games in all competitions last season as PSG successfully defended their Ligue 1 and Champions League titles.The teenager appeared in all four of Senegal's matches at the 2026 World Cup, netting in a 3-1 defeat by France to become the youngest African player to score at a men's World Cup.Mbaye joined PSG in the summer of 2018 from FC Versailles 78, progressing through their youth academy and making his senior debut in August 2024 at the age of 16.The winger was born in France and represented Les Bleus at youth level, but switched international allegiance to Senegal in 2025 after qualifying through his father.A product of Manchester City's youth academy, Harwood-Bellis joined Southampton for £20m in 2024 after impressing on loan.A loan spell at Burnley in 2022-23 ended with a Championship winner's medal, before he helped Southampton to promotion via the play-offs in 2023-24.Southampton finished bottom of the table in Harwood-Bellis' first season as a Premier League defender, before they reached the Championship play-off final last season.However, Southampton were disqualified after the Spygate scandal and began the current campaign with a four-point deduction.Harwood-Bellis apologised for making a binoculars gesture during their play-off semi-final second leg victory over Middlesbrough.Mbaye is the latest attacker to join Unai Emery's side following Alejandro Garnacho, Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson.Harwood-Bellis replaces Ezri Konsa in Villa's defence, after the England centre-back made a £55m move to defending Premier League champions Arsenal.While Villa have spent around £280m over the summer, Unai Emery has lost several key members of his Europa League-winning squad.The club have raised over £313m in player sales, including Morgan Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea and Ollie Watkins joining Al-Hilal for £51m.Aston Villa have committed to spend about £280m in Emery's summer rebuild. The arrivals of Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis on deadline day shows Villa are continuing to spend big. They have broken their transfer record twice with the arrivals of forwards Johan Manzambi (£52m) and Nicolas Jackson (£65m) so cannot plead poverty.If all clauses and add-ons are triggered Villa would be pushing £300m this summer, despite needing to sell to comply with Uefa and Premier League financial rules. Uefa limits the amount of revenue spent on wages, transfers and agent fees to 70% and Villa have already breached the regulations twice. They were fined £19.4m in June - with £12.9m suspended - having been hit with a £9.5m sanction for a similar breach the year before and need to ensure they break even because of their settlement agreement with Uefa.Despite that, Matteo Ruggeri (£17m), Harwood-Bellis (£30m), Joao Gomes (£38m) Jackson, Zion Suzuki (£30m), Manzambi and Mbaye (£47m) have all arrived, while  midfielder Leon Goretzka has also joined on a free transfer after leaving Bayern Munich.That comes having brought in just over £300m through the sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne, Emi Martinez, Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins. That figure also includes the £10.3m departure to Benfica of Enzo Barrenechea, who never played a Villa game, and Roma paying £21.3m to make Donyell Malen's loan permanent.Emery said following Monday's defeat at Arsenal he was happy with their transfer business, and that everything Villa had planned for they had achieved.It was always going to be a summer of change at Villa Park, although the depth of the transition with so many key players leaving is something Emery has already admitted he did not expect.

schema.headline: Aston Villa complete Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis signings

title: Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding
description: The government is to create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding. An investment of £110m, w
body: The government is to create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding. An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.Justice Secretary Alex Norris is also due to give more details in the Commons later on changes to the early release scheme, which aims to free up space in prisons as they near maximum capacity.He told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly."This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.But Chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."Norris said the government had delivered more than 3,200 prison places in two years.Investment on more prison spaces was announced in last year's spending review and the £110m is not new money, A £7bn capital investment plan to create 14,000 prison places by 2031. On the early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales, Norris said victims were being sent letters informing them and offered support from victim liaison officers.He insisted offenders would face restrictions on their release, including tagging and bans on attending football games.Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said victims wanted to know how these early releases would affect them, especially those who had faced domestic abuse or stalking.Plans for the early release scheme have been changed after concern about who would be freed.  Rapists, those found guilty of serious child sex offences and grooming offences were excluded. Then at the weekend Prime Minister Andy Burnham told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would also now be excluded, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.Burnham said this would mean hundreds more prisoners staying in jail and extra prison space would be created by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.Among those no longer eligible for early release is Shane Kelk, who was jailed after a hit-and-run crash which left 20-year-old Amy Cooper dead.Amy's mother Amanda originally received letters telling her Kelk could be released early.She said the prospect made her feel "sick" and that it would have "devalued" her daughter's life.The block was a "massive relief", she said, adding that she was still "upset and angry" that she and other families had "been put through a period of uncertainty".Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries which is the highest rate of deportations since 2017, a 12% increase on the previous year.Plans to release prisoners still serving indefinite sentences under Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) have been criticised by the Conservatives, who say this in itself poses a risk of dangerous prisoners being released.IPPs have not been imposed since 2012 but there are still prisoners in jail in England and Wales who were given them.They were used where prisoners were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released if the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public. But ending indefinite sentences for those still serving them would require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.

schema.headline: Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding

title: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy
description: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it loo
body: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral.For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding.What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit."This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders."It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area."Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC.Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day."My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network."Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck."But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy

title: We survived the Aberfan disaster as schoolchildren, but were told not to talk about it
description: Image caption, Janett was the only child on her street to return home from school on the day of the disasterByHuw ThomasBBC Wales correspondentReporti
body: Image caption, Janett was the only child on her street to return home from school on the day of the disasterByHuw ThomasBBC Wales correspondentReporting fromAberfan and Tony BrownBBC WalesUpdated 1 September 2026 06:12 BSTJanett Bickley almost stayed home from school on the morning of 21 October 1966.The eight-year-old had recently recovered from pneumonia, but she was determined to go in for the last day before half-term.Shortly after taking her seat at Pantglas Junior School, Janett was buried beneath tonnes of coal slurry from a collapsing tip. It engulfed the classrooms and killed 144 people, including 116 children.Sixty years later, Janett is one of the many survivors of the Aberfan disaster whose lives were shaped by what they experienced."I've always wanted to do something to pay back to the community because I think I owed something to the community, because I lived," she said.The sentiment is echoed by other Aberfan survivors, who went on to devote much of their lives to helping others through education, public service, community work and charity.Image source, Janett BickleyImage caption, Janett (front row, second left) with her nursery classmates in 1964. Many of the children in this photograph died in the disaster, two years laterJanett has a clear memory of the aftermath of the disaster.A classmate dug her out from the wreckage. She recalls climbing through broken rafters before joining a queue of children waiting to be pulled through a window to safety. Later, she discovered that she had been the only child from her street to return home from school that day.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, When a colliery waste tip collapsed, slurry crashed into Pantglas Junior School, killing 116 children and 28 adultsDespite the shared trauma, survivors rarely discussed what had happened."We were lucky, 'You lived, don't speak about it ever again'," Janett recalled being told.The message was repeated across many households."It wasn't discussed at all," she added. "We were way into our 30s or 40s before we even talked about it for the first time together."Image source, Janett BickleyImage caption, Janett in December 1967, a little over a year after the disasterFor Denise Morgan, the silence came after tragedy struck her own family.She had recently started grammar school after passing the 11-plus examination when her younger sister, Annette, was killed in the disaster. The shock and grief changed everything."When I came to take my O-levels as they were then, I failed them all miserably apart from one," she said. "The family were traumatised. My parents were traumatised."Image source, Family PhotoImage caption, Denise and her younger sister Annette, who was killed in the disasterFor decades, many survivors kept their memories private. Janett said children had often been encouraged to look forward rather than back."We all went to a psychiatrist, and we never spoke about it, even to the psychiatrist," said Denise.It was not until she was an adult, when former classmates began sharing their experiences, that some found relief."When we finally broke that seal of talking about it, it healed us, in a way," she said. Denise said many survivors had gone on to lead successful lives, while others had continued to struggle."You can see it in some people in Aberfan. They have come through it. Others have not, and suffered for many years."Image caption, Denise became a head teacher and was appointed an MBE for services to educationFor Denise, helping others began with a promise she made long before the disaster.As a pupil at Pantglas, she had been inspired by her teachers and decided she wanted to follow in their footsteps."I knew at 11 that I wanted to be a teacher," she said.But the path was far from straightforward.Grief affected her education, but she remained determined, and eventually she qualified, became a head teacher, and later received an MBE for services to education. Much of her career was spent supporting children from disadvantaged backgrounds and encouraging them to believe in their own potential."I often told my story," she said, sharing with schoolchildren: "You can be anything you want to be."Looking back today, she still thinks about the teachers she lost."They all helped to save many of the children that are alive today."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jeff Edwards was one of the last children to be pulled alive from Pantglas Junior School"They always contact us in Aberfan after the damage to see how we survived, how we coped," he said. "It's good to help others get through major disasters and traumas."Jeff believes his own response to Aberfan emerged years after the disaster.After establishing a career in accountancy and working in London, he returned home in the mid-1990s to find many local young people struggling in the aftermath of pit closures and industrial decline.Image caption, Jeff returned to Aberfan and feared a second generation of young people would be lost "I think the reason I really came back was those youngsters hanging about the street with no future. It was the second generation who were being lost to the community," he said.Many had left school without qualifications. Some were involved in crime, drugs and alcohol, and two local young people had taken their own lives.Using grants from organisations including Children in Need, Jeff helped to create projects focused on literacy, support for parents, employment and youth engagement. Some went on to transform lives, helping people into jobs and university.Jeff became adept at accessing grants and even had a donation from the late queen for one of his projects to help young people, though he cannot reveal the amount she sent."I've begged, stolen and borrowed to ensure that we've got the right resources for the young people of the village," he said.Later, as an independent councillor and then leader of the council, he helped secure funding for projects across Merthyr Tydfil and championed investment in education and community development.Looking back, he believes helping others also helped him."By helping them, I was helping myself, in terms of my own recovery process," he said.Image source, I.C. Rapoport/Getty ImagesImage caption, David Davies was pictured on the family farm near Pantglas Junior School in the weeks after the Aberfan disasterDavid Davies was sitting at his desk in Pantglas School when the tip collapsed. The debris knocked him unconscious."I was brought out and was initially placed with the deceased bodies and covered with a blanket in the playground area, until someone thought they saw my foot move," David recalled."I was evidently still alive and taken off to hospital where I was in intensive care for a little while. But actually I managed to get out of hospital in time for Bonfire night."David was the subject of photos by the renowned photographer Chuck Rapoport, who visited Aberfan in the days after the disaster.After recovering from serious head injuries, David attended a school outside the village and believed that separation from former classmates may have sheltered him from some of the trauma experienced by others."I did not witness anything that might have been going on around the school because I was unconscious. So I never had any ongoing issues with PTSD or anything like that, and thankfully I'd never had any long-term issues with my head injuries either," he said.David studied at Aberystwyth and Cambridge before building a successful career in international law.But after returning home, he increasingly devoted his time to public service.He became a magistrate, served with housing organisations and has spent 26 years as chair of the Aberfan memorial charity, which is responsible for preserving Aberfan's memorial sites.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, David took the Prince and Princess of Wales around the Aberfan memorial garden in 2023What motivates David remains clear."I'm clearly grateful to have survived an experience that half of my classmates did not," he said."It's really in their honour and in their memory that I'm driven forward, and have been over the last 26 years, to achieve fitting memorial sites both here at the memorial garden and the cemetery and other memorials to victims, so that they will be of a standard that will be fitting of their memory and acceptable to the community both here in Wales and further afield."He added: "I think the Queen put it in the words of 'an indomitable spirit' in the community. And I think that really sums it up in terms of what this community has gone through, how it's recovered, and the difference it's made to the community as a whole."Image caption, Janett recently got a tattoo of a clock that shows the time of the disasterFor Janett, the urge to give something back intensified during the Covid-19 pandemic.After a 30-year career in the pharmaceutical industry, she found herself looking out of her window and thinking about the isolation and loneliness affecting the community around her.Her campaign to install a Christmas tree in Aberfan soon grew into something much bigger.Working with volunteers, she helped secure funding for Christmas lights, community celebrations, carnival events and local projects designed to bring people together."The wellbeing of the community was ripped apart and it took a long time to build back up," she said.Today she also campaigns for the future of community facilities, supports local scouting and is working to ensure a community events organisation can continue after she steps back."All of a sudden the community is getting together, and I love it," she said.The disaster itself remains with her.Recently she had an image of a clock, frozen at 09:13 on 21 October 1966, tattooed on her arm."It is with me for life," said Janett.'We're lucky - we lived'Survivors and families who were affected by the Aberfan disaster have all done very different things with their lives, but many have found ways to honour those children who never had the chance to grow up.For Janett, it comes back to a simple belief."We feel lucky," she said."We're lucky we lived. Let's make this work. Let's do something for the community, because we're obviously here for a reason."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: We survived the Aberfan disaster as schoolchildren, but were told not to talk about it

title: How conviction of Duane Davis could help inspire efforts to find killer of Notorious B.I.G.
description: The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing: Davis' own words. Through documentaries with the media, his own me
body: The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing: Davis' own words. Through documentaries with the media, his own memoir, podcasts and even a secret police interview, he acknowledged his role in Shakur's death. Davis said he tossed a firearm in the backseat and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, used the gun to fatally shoot Shakur as they pulled up alongside his vehicle in Las Vegas on 7 September, 1996.Anderson was shot dead in 1998, having denied killing Shakur.During the trial, there were no eye-witnesses to place Davis as being in the car, no murder weapon presented, no video or photo evidence. His defence team went as far as to argue there wasn't even proof that he was in Las Vegas that night.Rahmani said it was a difficult case to prosecute. He noted the rumours and speculation surrounding Davis were nothing new and had been around for decades - but the decision to charge him and go to trial was an "uphill climb" - a gutsy move - for prosecutors. "Look, when you're a prosecutor, you're expected to win every time. They made a difficult decision to charge a case that a lot of people thought might be a loser," he explained. "And they got justice, where other people didn't even bother trying." Davis' attorney Michael Sanft asked the jury to consider "what facts do you have?" He urged the panel, before they decided their guilty verdict, to discredit his client as a liar who told tales to sell books and make money. "There's no proof," he argued to the jury. The moment the guilty verdict was read in court, there was an outpouring of emotion among Shakur's family. Some cried and wiped tears with tissues. Others hugged and held hands - one family member even embraced one of the prosecutors in the case. Trial attorney Shaun Kent said the case really evolved with each interview and moment that Davis decided to open his mouth and talk about the case more. "There are no other witnesses, besides him," Kent told the BBC before the trial, noting that the "strongest witness against him - is him". Rahmani said in his opinion, Davis would "go down as one of the world's dumbest criminals", who likely would have never have faced charges if he had stayed silent. "He really couldn't stop himself," Rahmani added. "Even when he was arrested and in custody, he was giving interviews." Much of the Shakur trial forced the jury to place themselves back to the 1990s, at a time of intense gang violence that had infiltrated roots into hip-hop music and rivalries between East-Coast and West-Coast rappers.It was a time of deep-rooted mistrust in policing and a street code that forbade snitching to authorities. Even Shakur, after being hit multiple times in the drive-by shooting that would later kill him, refused to talk to authorities. "We'll take care of it," he said in an ambulance as an officer tried to question him on who did it. The silence was echoed months later in the shooting death of Biggie Smalls. Biggie, one of the biggest East Coast rappers, was leaving an after-party in Los Angeles for the Soul Train Music Awards, when a black Chevrolet pulled up to his vehicle at a red light and opened fire on 9 March, 1997. It was almost exactly six months after the shooting that killed Shakur, one of the biggest West Coast rappers.Both were Grammy-nominated artists at the top of their genre, making millions and being played incessantly on the radio. They were also at the centre of a feud between East Coast and West Coast rap, that spilled over into their lyrics and also led to threats and physical violence. Both shootings led to no arrests, no convictions, just rumours and conspiracies and gang violence that exploded on the streets of Los Angeles as street gangs sought to hold one another accountable in the aftermath of both rappers' deaths. Like Shakur's death, countless theories and names have surrounded the death of Biggie in Los Angeles, but police with the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) have not made any arrests."It's really a stain on the LAPD. The fact that this could happen and not a single arrest was made and no one was prosecuted," Rahmani said, noting Biggie's killing happened on a public street in the middle of the second most populous US city. "Prosecutors don't like to lose and tend to be a little gun shy," Rahmani explained. "But, maybe this [Tupac's conviction] will embolden folks in Los Angeles to maybe take another look at it, a cold case that's coming up on 30 years." Asked about the cases and whether the Tupac murder conviction could revive Biggie's death, the LAPD told the BBC that it was aware of the conviction and the investigation into Biggie's case remained active. "The murder of Christopher Wallace remains an open, unsolved case within LAPD's Robbery-Homicide Division," Lt Elpidio Orozco said, urging anyone with any tips to call authorities.

schema.headline: How conviction of Duane Davis could help inspire efforts to find killer of Notorious B.I.G.

title: Ukraine war: What to make of Modi's plea to Putin to end conflict
description: If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war
body: If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly? The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses. Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries. But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats. As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.He didn't. And he hasn't.There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."Polite, but vague. And non-committal.After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.And "moving forward" at what pace?And, crucially, on which path?All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: What to make of Modi's plea to Putin to end conflict

title: Liberals sweep three seats in boost for Carney after trade tensions with US
description: Mark Carney's Liberal Party won all three parliamentary special elections that were held in Canada on Monday, indicating ongoing public support for th
body: Mark Carney's Liberal Party won all three parliamentary special elections that were held in Canada on Monday, indicating ongoing public support for the prime minister well into his second year in office and after recent trade tensions with the US. The votes were triggered by the resignations of three MPs. The most notable result saw Carney's party claim a Québec seat previously held by an opposition Conservative.In the other two votes, in Ontario and British Columbia, the Liberals held onto their seats as pollsters expected.Carney has received a bump in the polls following his decision to end trade talks with the US, accusing Canada's southern neighbour of proposing terms that were "unfair".The prime minister congratulated the three victorious Liberal candidates in a post on X. Reflecting on the wider issues facing his premiership, he wrote: "Canada is being tested in a changing world, and Canadians are up for it."The results mean Carney will keep his slim majority in the House of Commons. Canadian media projected a sizeable victory for the Liberals in the Québec district of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord. Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil, a dairy farmer, becomes the district's new MP, having claimed more than half of the overall vote.He beat the Bloc Québécois and the Conservatives into second and third places respectively. The seat had been a narrow three-way race last time round.Addressing his supporters in French, Gobeil said "this victory means we can maintain Canadian unity all across the country", CBC reported.Elsewhere, Tanveer Shahnawaz won his contest in Beaches-East York, Ontario, and Braeden Caley emerged victorious from the race in North Vancouver-Capilano, British Columbia.The Conservatives have struggled to close the gap with the Liberals since losing last year's federal election, with the latest polls suggesting they are trailing behind Carney's party by about 10 points. Four members of their ranks crossed the floor to the governing Liberals since the April 2025 election, and three others have either resigned or have announced plans to do so.Richard Martel, the former Conservative MP of the Quebec constituency that held Monday's by-election, stepped down last month after he was appointed by Carney to Canada's Senate. Senators in Canada are not elected. The loss of Martel's seat to the Liberals is another blow to Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, who won a leadership test in January by a landslide but has faced questions about his ability to navigate the current political climate in Canada. Meanwhile, the approval of Carney's government rose four points in recent weeks, as has the prime minister's personal popularity, according to figures released on Monday by Canadian pollster Abacus Data, external.David Coletto, founder of Abacus Data, credits this boost to US President Donald Trump's lack of popularity with Canadians, as well as the country rallying around Carney's decision to walk away from trade talks with the White House. This trend is most pronounced in Quebec, Coletto wrote in a note on Monday, where "Carney's personal rating is stronger there than anywhere else in the country".Quebec stands to be one of the most provinces most affected by Trump's new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, which came into effect after trade talks collapsed earlier this month. In a recent report, global forecasting firm Oxford Economics warned that Quebec could lose C$2bn ($1.4bn; £1bn) in annual output by 2028.

schema.headline: Liberals sweep three seats in boost for Carney after trade tensions with US
